newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Biotech forum hears calls for ethics watchdog.
newsitem.headline: Biotech forum hears calls for ethics watchdog.

text.p: The European Federation of Biotechnology (EFB) came under pressure at its congress on Tuesday to set up a disciplinary watchdog to allay public fears that its members may abuse new discoveries in genetic engineering.

"Biotechnology has reached the stage where we now require a corporate body which can be responsible for the licensing of...individuals, for promulgating a code of conduct and bringing discipline to those who transgress this code," Ray Spier of the University of Surrey, in Britain, told delegates.

Biotechnology -- which Spier defined as the use of genetically engineered organisms as products and services -- has come under close scrutiny since scientists in Scotland reported earlier this year they had cloned a lamb -- which they named Dolly -- from a single cell taken from an adult sheep.
Their success raised the prospect that the procedure could be used to make humans genetically identical to an existing person.
Industry experts say Europe's biotechnology industry is booming with 15 percent annual growth.
However, a survey to be discussed at the four-day congress shows that most Europeans do not trust their governments to protect them from the possible dangers of genetically modified food.

The sample, taken among 16,000 people across the European Union, shows 74 percent of the population want labelling on such products and only 28 percent think regulation should be left to the industry, while 60 percent think only traditional breeding methods should be used for farm animals.
Images of Frankenstein and eugenics were frequently invoked, the researchers said.

Spier said that as most biotechnologists work for companies they were more susceptible to conflicts of interest than other professions such as architects, doctors and lawyers, increasing the need for strong self-regulation.

He appealed for a European Union-backed biotechnologists' chartered institute which could bar from the profession practitioners who do not "use their knowledge and skills to bring benefit to society, the public and the environment".

However, Spier's appeal to the EFB to set up an ethics committee on the style of the British Medical Association was opposed by some scientists on the grounds that there was an insufficiently clear definition of what biotechnology actually is.
"If a biotechnologist is barred, what is he barred from?" asked Claus Emborg, professor of biotechnology of the Technical University of Denmark.
"When you are a lawyer and when you are a doctor it is defined what you are allowed to do but as a biotechnologist you can do anything and anybody can do the things we do."

Bernard Dixon, chairman of the EFB's task group on public perceptions, said much of the EFB's resistance to self-regulation came from a difficulty in adjusting to recent changes in the scientist's role in society.

"A lot of people started their careers when scientists didn't have to worry too much about the public outside the laboratory walls," he told Reuters. "The scientific community has not addressed this (ethical) issue properly -- now they are having to."
The EFB congress, which continues until Thursday, will debate the watchdog proposals, but Spier said it could take up to five years to adopt his ideas.
"The EFB has been offered an opportunity," he said. "But the federation has several hundred member societies and it can't move faster than those member societies."
